claims.claim: William Nordhaus published the reconstruction of the long-run price of lighting ('Do Real-Output and Real-Wage Measures Capture Reality? The History of Lighting Suggests Not', 1996).
claims.episode_span: Nordhaus’s reconstruction shows that once the service is counted in lumens rather than in lamps or gallons, the price trajectory becomes visible as a series of discrete attacks on the dominant loss mechanism.
claims.source_title: Do Real-Output and Real-Wage Measures Capture Reality? The History of Lighting Suggests Not - NBER
claims.supporting_quote: Do Real-Output and Real-Wage Measures Capture Reality? The History of Lighting Suggests Not William D. Nordhaus

claims.claim: The price of lighting has fallen enormously over the long run: in the UK, from around £34,000 per million lumen-hours (1300s, in 2000 prices) to £2.15 by 2023 - a 16,000-fold decline.
claims.episode_span: By the early twenty-first century the cost per megalumen-hour had fallen by something like four orders of magnitude from 1800 levels when measured in constant dollars and constant purchasing power.
claims.source_title: Light at Night - Our World in Data
claims.supporting_quote: In the 1300s, one million units of lighting — a lumen-hour — would have cost around £34,000 in 2000 prices. By 2023, this had fallen to £2.15. That is a 16,000-fold decline.

claims.claim: Incandescent bulbs convert less than 5% of consumed energy into visible light; the rest is released as heat/infrared.
claims.episode_span: even so, roughly 95 percent of the electrical input still emerged as infrared
claims.supporting_quote: Less than 5% of the energy they consume is converted into visible light; the rest is released as heat.

claims.claim: Fluorescent lamps achieve a luminous efficacy of roughly 50-100 lm/W, several times better than incandescents.
claims.episode_span: raising system efficacy from roughly 15 lm/W to 60–80 lm/W
claims.supporting_quote: These are more efficient than incandescent lights, having a luminous efficacy from 50 to 100 lm/W (depending on the structure, type of phosphor and type of ballast used)

claims.claim: Modern production white LED lamps exceed 150 lm/W; the most efficient commercial LED lamps exceed 200 lm/W.
claims.episode_span: modern phosphor-converted white LEDs exceed 150 lm/W in production devices
claims.supporting_quote: The most efficient commercially available LED lamps have efficiencies exceeding 200 lumens per watt (lm/W) and convert more than half the input power into light.

claims.claim: The theoretical limit for a phosphor-mixed white LED is about 260-300 lm/W.
claims.episode_span: a rough estimate places the theoretical maximum around 250–300 lm/W for a broadband white spectrum once all non-radiative paths are removed
claims.supporting_quote: Theoretical limit for a white LED with phosphorescence color mixing 260 – 300
